entry.title: Germany’s Raider That Captured an Entire Whaling Fleet: Hilfskreuzer Pinguin (1941)

media:group.media:title: Germany’s Raider That Captured an Entire Whaling Fleet: Hilfskreuzer Pinguin (1941)
media:group.media:description:
In June 1940 a converted freighter slipped out of Germany under a false name, armed, disguised, and ordered to attack Allied shipping wherever found.
Over the next eleven months she worked the South Atlantic, the Indian Ocean and the edge of the Antarctic ice under Kapitän zur See Ernst-Felix Krüder.
By May 1941 the Royal Navy knew a raider was operating in the Indian Ocean, and the cruiser HMS Cornwall was sent to find her.

entry.title: America’s Most Aggressive Submarine: Dudley Morton’s USS Wahoo, 1943 - Animated

media:group.media:title: America’s Most Aggressive Submarine: Dudley Morton’s USS Wahoo, 1943 - Animated
media:group.media:description:
✨ Use my link to join Freecash and receive a $10,- bonus for completing your first task: https://signupfreecash.com/houseofhistory
By 1943, USS Wahoo had become one of the most aggressive American submarines in the Pacific, with Commander Dudley “Mush” Morton and executive officer Richard O’Kane pushing close to Japanese shipping routes from the Yellow Sea to the waters around Hokkaido.
Her patrols brought rapid attacks, risky surface chases, and a growing reputation at a time when the American submarine campaign was becoming one of the main threats to Japan’s maritime lifelines.
In October 1943, Morton took Wahoo north again, into the Sea of Japan and toward the narrow passage beside Cape Soya. The boat never returned, and her final movements remained uncertain for more than six decades, until the wreck was identified in La Perouse Strait in 2006.
